title: XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM, VARIANT TYPE
alt_titles: XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM WITH NORMAL DNA REPAIR RATES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that xeroderma pigmentosum, variant type (XPV) is caused by mutation in the gene encoding DNA polymerase eta (POLH, also called hRAD30). In one family, the patient had inherited two different missense mutations, one from each heterozygous parent.

checks.claim: Xeroderma pigmentosum, variant type (XPV) is caused by mutation in the gene encoding DNA polymerase eta (POLH).
checks.evidence_quote: These results indicate that defects in hRAD30 cause XP-V
checks.explanation: Abstract states hRAD30 defects cause XP-V; POLH/DNA polymerase eta is the approved nomenclature for hRAD30 (the abstract itself does not use the name 'polymerase eta').

checks.claim: The POLH gene is also called hRAD30.
checks.evidence_quote: XP variant (XP-V) cell lines harbor nonsense or frameshift mutations in hRAD30, the human counterpart of yeast RAD30
checks.explanation: Paper uses the alias hRAD30; equating it with approved symbol POLH is standard nomenclature.

checks.claim: In one XPV family, the patient had inherited two different POLH missense mutations, one from each heterozygous parent.
checks.evidence_quote: In one family, we confirmed inheritance of two heterozygous mis-sense mutations.
checks.explanation: The abstract says two missense mutations were inherited in one family with heterozygous parents, but it does not name the gene (POLH).

paragraphs.text: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XPV) is an inherited disorder associated with clinical photosensitivity and an increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers (Masutani et al., 1999; Itoh et al., 2000). Unlike cells from patients in the excision-repair-deficient groups of xeroderma pigmentosum (XP-A to XP-G), XPV cells carry out normal nucleotide excision repair but are defective in replication of ultraviolet-damaged DNA, i.e., in postreplication repair (Lehmann et al., 1975; Masutani et al., 1999).

checks.claim: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XPV) is an inherited disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) is an inherited disorder which is associated with increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers.

checks.claim: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XPV) is associated with clinical photosensitivity.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum variant show clinical photosensitivity

checks.claim: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XPV) is associated with an increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers.
checks.evidence_quote: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) is an inherited disorder which is associated with increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers.

checks.claim: Unlike cells from the excision-repair-deficient xeroderma pigmentosum groups (XP-A to XP-G), XPV cells carry out normal nucleotide excision repair.
checks.evidence_quote: Unlike other xeroderma pigmentosum cells (belonging to groups XP-A to XP-G), XP-V cells carry out normal nucleotide-excision repair processes

checks.claim: XPV cells are defective in replication of ultraviolet-damaged DNA, i.e., in postreplication repair.
checks.evidence_quote: but are defective in their replication of ultraviolet-damaged DNA.
checks.explanation: The abstract says XP-V cells are defective in replicating UV-damaged DNA, but it does not use the term 'postreplication repair.' That label probably comes from the other paper cited (Lehmann et al., 1975).

paragraphs.text: The 'pigmented xerodermoid' had been defined on the basis of mild clinical symptoms suggesting a condition similar to but distinct from xeroderma pigmentosum. Cleaver et al. (1980) compared XP and pigmented xerodermoid cell cultures after ultraviolet irradiation, measuring unscheduled DNA synthesis, strand breakage during repair, chain growth during semiconservative DNA replication with or without caffeine, and recovery of DNA replication. They concluded that a pigmented xerodermoid cell culture was indistinguishable from the XP variant and that the term pigmented xerodermoid was therefore redundant.

checks.evidence_quote: The "pigmented xerodermoid" was previously defined on the basis of mild clinical symptoms that suggested it might be similar to but distinct from xeroderma pigmentosum (XP).

checks.claim: Cleaver et al. (1980) compared XP and pigmented xerodermoid cell cultures after UV irradiation by measuring unscheduled DNA synthesis, strand breakage during repair, chain growth during semiconservative DNA replication with or without caffeine, and recovery of DNA replication.

checks.explanation: The abstract lists the same four measurements.

checks.evidence_quote: the XP variant and the former term is therefore redundant.
checks.explanation: "The former term" is "pigmented xerodermoid", so the claim matches.

paragraphs.text: Lehmann et al. (1975) found that cells from the class of xeroderma pigmentosum patients whose cells are completely normal in excision repair of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers have an abnormality in DNA synthesis after UV irradiation. The time taken to convert the initially low-molecular-weight DNA synthesized in UV-irradiated cells into high-molecular-weight DNA was much greater in these variants than in normal cells, and this slow conversion was drastically inhibited by caffeine, which had no effect in normal cells. Two cell lines from excision-repair-defective classes of XP showed intermediate effects.

checks.evidence_quote: There is, however, one class of these patients whose cells are completely normal in this excision repair process. We have found that these cells have an abnormality in the manner in which DNA is synthesized after UV-irradiation.

checks.evidence_quote: The time taken to convert initially low-molecular-weight DNA synthesized in UV-irradiated cells into high-molecular-weight DNA similar in size to that in untreated cells is much greater in these variants than in normal cells.

checks.claim: Lehmann et al. (1975) found that the slow conversion of low- to high-molecular-weight DNA in XP variant cells was drastically inhibited by caffeine.
checks.evidence_quote: Furthermore, this slow conversion of low to high-molecular-weight newly synthesized DNA is drastically inhibited by caffeine, which has no effect in normal cells.

checks.evidence_quote: Two cell lines from classes of xeroderma pigmentosum that are defective in excision-repair show intermediate effects

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1991) noted that XP variant cells are only slightly more sensitive than normal cells to the cytotoxic effect of UV radiation but significantly more sensitive to its mutagenic effect. When an XP variant cell line was transfected with a UV-irradiated shuttle vector carrying the supF gene, the frequency of mutants increased linearly with dose, with a slope 5 times steeper than that seen with normal cells. Of 53 independent mutants, 52 contained base substitutions, and 62 of 64 substitutions involved a dipyrimidine. Twenty-eight percent of the mutations involved A:T base pairs, mostly at position 136, compared with only 11% in normal cells. Wang et al. (1991) suggested that XP variant cells are less likely than normal cells to incorporate dAMP opposite bases involved in photoproducts, which could account for their UV hypermutability.

checks.evidence_quote: Twenty-eight percent of the mutations involved A.T base pairs, with the majority found at position 136, the middle of a run of three A.T base pairs. (In the normal cells, this value was only 11%.)

checks.claim: The A:T base-pair mutations in supF in the XP variant cell line were mostly at position 136.

checks.claim: Wang et al. (1991) suggested that XP variant cells are less likely than normal cells to incorporate dAMP opposite bases involved in photoproducts, which could account for their UV hypermutability.

checks.explanation: This matches the authors' stated conclusion. The paper frames it more tentatively, as conditional on equal excision rates and on the same thing happening in chromosomal DNA, but 'suggested' reflects that adequately.

paragraphs.text: Johnson et al. (1999) noted that xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive disease. Itoh et al. (2000) found that the clinically unaffected parents of an XPV patient were each heterozygous for a different missense mutation inherited by the patient, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.evidence_quote: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by a high incidence of skin cancers.

checks.evidence_quote: In one family, we confirmed inheritance of two heterozygous mis-sense mutations.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports inheritance of two heterozygous missense mutations from heterozygous parents. It does not explicitly say the parents were clinically unaffected.

checks.claim: The inheritance of XPV in the family studied by Itoh et al. (2000) is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: Cells from heterozygotic parents showed normal levels of unscheduled DNA synthesis, recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis
checks.explanation: Heterozygous parents and an affected child fit recessive inheritance, but the abstract never states autosomal recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Using a cell-free assay for translesion DNA synthesis, Masutani et al. (1999) isolated from HeLa cells a DNA polymerase that continues replication on damaged DNA by bypassing UV-induced thymine dimers in XP-V cell extracts. They showed that this polymerase is a human homolog of the yeast Rad30 protein, DNA polymerase eta. All XP-V cells examined carried mutations in the DNA polymerase eta gene, and recombinant human DNA polymerase eta corrected the inability of XP-V cell extracts to replicate DNA by bypassing thymine dimers.

checks.evidence_quote: Using an improved cell-free assay for trans-lesion DNA synthesis, we have recently isolated a DNA polymerase from HeLa cells that continues replication on damaged DNA by bypassing ultraviolet-induced thymine dimers in XP-V cell extracts.

checks.evidence_quote: Here we show that this polymerase is a human homologue of the yeast Rad30 protein, recently identified as DNA polymerase eta.

checks.evidence_quote: We found that all XP-V cells examined carry mutations in their DNA polymerase eta gene.

paragraphs.text: Johnson et al. (1999) found that XP-V cell lines harbored nonsense or frameshift mutations in hRAD30, the human counterpart of yeast RAD30, which encodes a DNA polymerase involved in error-free bypass of UV damage. Of the 8 mutations identified, 7 would result in a severely truncated hRad30 protein.

paragraphs.text: In 1 of 2 Japanese families with XPV, Itoh et al. (2000) confirmed inheritance of 2 heterozygous missense mutations in the POLH gene: a 1840A-G transition resulting in a lys535-to-glu (K535E) substitution, and a 2003A-C transversion resulting in a missense change at lys589. Neither mutation was found in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals.

checks.explanation: Two families are stated. That they were Japanese is only implied by the use of Japanese controls.

checks.evidence_quote: In one family, we confirmed inheritance of two heterozygous mis-sense mutations.
checks.explanation: Stated, but the abstract does not name the POLH gene.

checks.explanation: The variant details match. The gene name and the family's Japanese origin are not stated in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Cleaver et al. (1980) concluded that the defect in XP variant cells appears to be the loss of a gene product that permits normal cells to replicate DNA without interruption at UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, so that replication forks are blocked more frequently and at lower doses in XP variant cells. They suggested that the correlation between this defect and the high levels of actinic carcinogenesis in these patients pointed to an important role for perturbations in DNA replication in human carcinogenesis.

checks.evidence_quote: The defect common to these cell types appears to be the loss of a gene product that permits normal cells to replicate DNA without interruption at damaged sites (u.v.-induced pyrimidine dimers).
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly. It calls it the defect shared by both cell types, and that includes the XP variant.

checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly. The draft's "UV doses" follows from the UV-irradiation context.

checks.claim: Cleaver et al. (1980) suggested that the correlation between the XP variant replication defect and high levels of actinic carcinogenesis pointed to an important role for perturbations in DNA replication in human carcinogenesis.
checks.evidence_quote: The correlation between this defect and high levels of actinic carcinogenesis in these patients points to an important role for perturbations in DNA replication in human carcinogenesis.

paragraphs.text: Using DNA combing, Despras et al. (2010) showed that the translesion synthesis defect in XP-V cells leads to a strong reduction in the number of active replication forks and a high proportion of stalled forks. Extensive regions of single-strand DNA formed during replication in irradiated XP-V cells, leading to overactivation of the ATR/Chk1 pathway after low UVC doses. A low concentration of caffeine added after irradiation significantly decreased Chk1 activation and abrogated DNA synthesis in XP-V cells, and inhibition of Chk1 by UCN-01 aggravated the replication defect by increasing fork stalling and sensitized XP-V cells to UVC as caffeine does. They concluded that pol-eta acts at stalled forks to resume their progression, and that in its absence Chk1 kinase becomes essential for replication resumption via fork stabilization.

paragraphs.text: Itoh et al. (1996) described a simple autoradiographic method for diagnosing XPV that measures 3 cellular markers after UV irradiation in patient fibroblasts compared with adjacent normal cells: unscheduled DNA synthesis, recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis. Among hereditary photosensitive disorders, including xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and UV-sensitive syndrome, only XPV cells showed normal unscheduled DNA synthesis and normal recovery of RNA synthesis but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis (approximately 50% of control), a reduction enhanced in the presence of caffeine.

checks.explanation: The abstract describes a simple autoradiographic method for diagnosing XPV.

checks.claim: The autoradiographic XPV diagnostic method of Itoh et al. (1996) measures unscheduled DNA synthesis, recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV irradiation in patient fibroblasts compared with adjacent normal cells.

checks.explanation: The abstract names all three markers and states that patient fibroblasts are compared with adjacent normal cells.

checks.claim: Among hereditary photosensitive disorders including xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and UV-sensitive syndrome, only XPV cells showed normal unscheduled DNA synthesis and normal recovery of RNA synthesis but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis.

paragraphs.text: Itoh et al. (2000) reported that recovery of replicative DNA synthesis in XPV cells was 51 +/- 6% of normal, reduced to 36 +/- 5% in the presence of a nontoxic level of caffeine. Cells from heterozygous parents in 2 families showed normal unscheduled DNA synthesis, recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis, but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis in the presence of 1 mM caffeine (53 +/- 8% of normal control). In colony-forming assays, heterozygous cells showed normal UV survival without caffeine but slightly reduced survival with 1 mM caffeine. The authors suggested that XPV heterozygotes can be identified by their sensitivity to UV irradiation in the presence of nontoxic levels of caffeine.

paragraphs.text: In the differential diagnosis, Fujiwara et al. (1981) studied an 8-year-old boy (UV81KO) with only acute recurrent sunburns and lowered minimal erythema doses, whose fibroblasts were 5-fold more sensitive than normal to 254-nm UV killing and showed defective recovery of DNA synthesis after UV irradiation, but no detectable defect in nucleotide excision repair or in replicative bypass (molecular-weight increase of pulse-chased DNA). Baseline sister chromatid exchanges were elevated (10-12 SCEs/cell vs 5 in normal cells). On the basis of clinical, cellular, and molecular characteristics, the authors distinguished this disorder from xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and Bloom syndrome and proposed it as a new photodermatosis.

checks.evidence_quote: A non-sensitive, 8-yr-old male patient (termed UV81KO) with only acute recurrent sunburns and without any other physical or neuromental retardations was studied.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes an 8-year-old boy, called UV81KO, whose only symptom was acute recurrent sunburns.

checks.claim: Patient UV81KO had lowered minimal erythema doses.
checks.evidence_quote: The patient's skin exhibited lowered minimal erythema doses between 280 and 300 nm monochromatic wavelengths without delayed peaking of erythema.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports lowered minimal erythema doses.

checks.claim: Baseline sister chromatid exchanges in patient UV81KO cells were elevated (10-12 SCEs/cell vs 5 in normal cells).

paragraphs.text: In a Japanese patient with xeroderma pigmentosum variant, Itoh et al. (2000) identified an A-to-G transition at nucleotide 1840 of the POLH gene, resulting in a lys535-to-glu (K535E) substitution, inherited from a heterozygous parent, together with a second missense mutation (2003A-C) at lys589. agent.process_note: I read all 11 files. Nine are abstracts only, and two (Cleaver 1972 and Robbins et al. 1974) are titles only. The causal gene (DNA polymerase eta / hRAD30) comes from Masutani et al. (1999) and Johnson et al. (1999). The only specific variants given are the two missense mutations in Itoh et al. (2000). The protein change for the 2003A-C mutation is stated only as 'K589', so the new amino acid is not specified. No gene MIM number or chromosomal location was supplied, and none appears in the papers, so both are left out. The symbol POLH is used as standard nomenclature; the papers call the gene DNA polymerase eta / hRAD30. Robbins et al. (1974) concerns XP generally and was not cited. Fujiwara et al. (1981) was cited only for differential diagnosis.
